bearings.system_side: desk_roi in fec/surfaces/make_member_desk.py returns expected weighted flips gained from the next 10k increment (CHUNK) of CU money on a member. The dashboard head-to-head block solves for the CU money that offsets competitor spend. Neither is a firm return on lobbying dollars.
bearings.transfer_conditions: No numeric transfer. The paper numerator is a firm tax benefit from a one-time provision and the denominator is LDA spend (upper bound). Melange numerator is modeled member movement and denominator is FEC PAC money. Any quote needs the window FY2004-2006, the 93-firm denominator, and the median 172 next to the mean 869. The bearing describes the PAC side as capped at 10k; the code uses 10000 as a marginal increment, so describe it as a per-10k increment.
bearings.verifier_note: Every Table 6 figure and text quote matches (220, 257, 154, 869, 172.2, 243, 62.05bn, 282.7M, 93 firms, 39/54 split, fn 97 and fn 100). Softened only on the cap wording for the PAC side. The introduction states 62.5bn savings, which differs from Table 6.

bearings.transfer_conditions: These are firm-level predictors of capturing a 2004-2006 benefit in a cross-sectional design with no causal identification. They are weak support for a firm-size covariate and say nothing about sector-year giving or growth. Cite as single-era and cross-sectional. Any pooled coefficient over the industry fault line needs strata or an UNSTRATIFIED label.
bearings.verifier_note: All Table 3 and Table 5 coefficients and p-values match the text. The industry-predictive claim in the abstract is contradicted by Table 3 (no significant industry indicator) and only weakly supported by SIC 3800 at p=.085 in Table 5. The code lines exist and describe the same series. The regression design and the claimed growth results were not verified. The qualifies relation is overstated because the paper is firm-level and does not speak to sector-year growth.

bearings.paper_claim: Five firms lobbied against the AJCA for alternative tax plans and are not counted in the lobbying group (fn 99, p.28). A sensitivity analysis drops five repatriating lobbyists with uncertain support and raises ROI to 228:1 (fn 100, p.30). Coalition lobbyists out-returned solo lobbyists (257 vs 154). The paper does not describe the provision as lacking organized counter-lobbying.
bearings.system_side: fec/lobbying/contested_bills.py is a per-bill standard, advisory or contested registry. Its docstring gives ratification 2026-07-31, contested records supply an explicit per-bill counterparty set, and no consumer reads it yet (CONTESTED_V1 is planned). Verified.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports only a design implication: returns on a provision with little organized opposition may overstate what contested bills would show. The counter-lobbying evidence is five firms on the other side, so the uncontested label should be softened to five firms lobbied against it. The paper never studies contested bills.
bearings.verifier_note: Coalition figures match Table 6. The no-organized-counter-lobby claim is not in the paper and is partly contradicted by fn 99, which says five firms lobbied against the AJCA and four of them repatriated anyway. The system description is accurate. The fn 99 and fn 100 groups are different sets and should not be merged.

summary_issues: Summary says size, profitability and operating cash flow predict how much was repatriated. In Table 5 the pre-tax income indicator is not significant (-.314, p=.330). Profitability predicts only the repatriation decision (logit, p=.001).

Summary says the upper-bound denominator would double-count in-house and outside-firm LDA dollars. The paper never discusses an in-house vs outside-firm split. Its double-count risk comes from coding lobbying across several categories (fn 97). The Mentat concern is the analyst's inference, not the paper's.

Summary says the biggest returns came on an essentially uncontested provision. Footnote 99 reports five firms that lobbied against the AJCA, four of which repatriated anyway. Uncontested is an inference, not a finding.
Summary omits the introduction's numeric discrepancies: 496 repatriating firms (p.3) vs 476 in Sec. II (p.18), and 62.5bn savings (p.3) vs 62.05bn in Table 6. These should be noted.

Summary's paul_alignment asserts Paul's views (calls the figure an outlier, has ROI enthusiasm, his note is stale). The item's paul_entries contain no takeaways or annotations, so these statements have no support in the item file and should be removed or sourced.
Summary says the repat! search identified 476 repatriating firms. The search flagged 1,350 candidate firms; 476 firms reported repatriating (Group 1). Wording should say so.

Footnote 99 (five firms that lobbied against, excluded from the lobbying group) and footnote 100 (five repatriating lobbyists with uncertain support; ROI 228 when excluded) are different sets. The bearings conflate them.

Table 1 Panel A shows repatriators held significantly less cash (cash/assets 15 vs 20 percent), which sits awkwardly with the positive OLS cash coefficient in Table 5. The paper does not reconcile this. Noted, not an error in the summary.

Summary's headline figures (220:1, 257, 154, 869, median 172, 243, N=434, adj R2 .48, the cash inconsistency) all check out against the text. Coverage: all four bearings and all six related links were checked. Key_findings and paul_markup are not in this output schema and were not returned.
